paragraphs.en: For most of human history, the overwhelming majority of people lived in the countryside. That balance has now shifted decisively. It is widely reported that, at some point in the first decade of this century, the number of people living in urban areas overtook the rural population for the first time, and demographers expect the urban share to keep rising for decades, with most of the growth concentrated in Asia and Africa. The process, known as urbanisation, is among the defining transformations of the modern era, yet its consequences remain the subject of lively debate among economists, planners and the residents of cities themselves.

Explanations of why people move to cities typically distinguish between push and pull factors. On the one hand, rural life may offer limited prospects: farm incomes are often low and unpredictable, land may be divided into ever smaller plots between heirs, and a drought or flood can wipe out a year's work. On the other hand, cities appear to promise higher wages, a wider range of jobs and better access to schools and hospitals. Migrants do not always find what they were hoping for, but for many the decision is a rational calculation: even an insecure urban job may pay more than agricultural labour, and the presence of relatives who have already made the move can ease the transition considerably.

Economists have long argued that cities are not merely large collections of people but engines of productivity. When firms, workers and suppliers are concentrated in one place, they benefit from what are known as agglomeration economies. Businesses can draw on a deep pool of skilled labour, workers can change employers without relocating, and ideas spread more rapidly through informal contact. It is partly for this reason that a disproportionate share of national output in many countries is generated in a handful of large cities. Density also makes certain services cheaper to provide per person, since a single water main or bus route can serve thousands of households.

Rapid growth, however, frequently outpaces the capacity of governments to plan for it. When new arrivals cannot afford formal housing, they often build their own homes on land they do not legally own, typically on the urban fringe or on sites considered unsuitable for construction, such as steep slopes or riverbanks prone to flooding. Such informal settlements now house a very large number of people worldwide. Living conditions in them vary enormously, but residents commonly lack secure tenure, adequate sanitation and reliable access to clean water, and the constant threat of eviction discourages them from investing in their homes.

It would be misleading, however, to regard informal settlements purely as places of misery. Many are vibrant communities with active local economies, in which residents run shops, workshops and services and gradually improve their dwellings as their incomes rise. Some urban planners now argue that demolishing such neighbourhoods and relocating their inhabitants to distant housing estates has often done more harm than good, cutting people off from jobs and social networks. Instead, they advocate upgrading in place: providing legal title, paved roads, drainage and electricity while allowing communities to remain where they are.

Even in more prosperous cities, growth places considerable strain on infrastructure. Roads become congested, public transport is overcrowded, and the cost of housing may rise faster than incomes, pushing lower-paid workers ever further from their jobs. Air pollution, much of it caused by traffic and heating, is a persistent problem in many large cities. Because major infrastructure takes years to plan, finance and build, cities that grow quickly are often perpetually catching up, investing to meet yesterday's demand rather than tomorrow's.

Whether urbanisation proves beneficial thus depends less on the movement of people itself than on how it is managed. Cities that invest early in transport, coordinate the use of land and include informal neighbourhoods in their plans appear better able to translate density into prosperity. Those that do not risk concentrating poverty rather than reducing it. The question for policymakers is therefore not whether to allow urban growth, which is in any case largely unstoppable, but how to ensure that its benefits are widely shared.
